section.title: The Words of Agur
section.sectionRationale: A distinct new voice speaks here, Agur son of Jakeh, otherwise unknown to Scripture, whose oracle opens with a confession of ignorance before God and moves through a prayer for honest daily bread, a string of vivid numerical sayings, and closes with a warning against self-exaltation and stirred up anger.
section.thesis: True wisdom begins by confessing how little we know before the incomprehensible God, asking for neither poverty nor riches but daily bread, and observing the world closely enough to see both the horror of certain evils and the humble genius written into ants, badgers, and locusts.
section.frameNote: Six clusters: Agur's confession of ignorance and the mystery of God and His Son; every word of God is flawless, and the prayer for honest bread; generations of evil and things never satisfied; wonders too great to understand, and the adulteress who feels no shame; small creatures who are exceedingly wise; stately creatures, and the folly of self-exaltation.

units.label: Agur's confession of ignorance
units.note: the mystery of God and His Son

verses.text:
These are the words of Agur son of Jakeh, the burden that this man declared to Ithiel: 
"I am weary, O God, and worn out.
Surely I am the most ignorant of men, and I lack the understanding of a man.
I have not learned wisdom, and I have no knowledge of the Holy One.

Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in His hands? Who has bound up the waters in His cloak? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is His name, and what is the name of His Son, surely you know!

units.label: Every word of God is flawless

verses.text: Every word of {{eloah|God}} is flawless; He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him.
Do not add to His words, lest He rebuke you and prove you a liar.
Two things I ask of You, do not refuse me before I die:

Keep falsehood and deceitful words far from me. Give me neither poverty nor riches; 
feed me with the bread that is my portion.
Otherwise, I may have too much and deny You, saying, 'Who is the LORD?' Or I may become poor and steal, profaning the name of my God.
Do not slander a servant to his master, or he will curse you, and you will bear the guilt.
There is a generation of those who curse their fathers and do not bless their mothers.
There is a generation of those who are pure in their own eyes and yet unwashed of their filth.
There is a generation, how haughty are their eyes and pretentious are their glances,
there is a generation whose teeth are swords and whose jaws are knives, devouring the oppressed from the earth and the needy from among men.

The leech has two daughters: Give and Give. 
There are three things that are never satisfied, four that never say, 'Enough!':

Sheol, 
the barren womb, 
land never satisfied with water, 
and fire that never says, 'Enough!'

units.label: Wonders too great to understand
units.note: the adulteress who feels no shame

verses.text: As for the eye that mocks a father and scorns obedience to a mother, may the ravens of the valley pluck it out and young vultures devour it.
There are three things too wonderful for me, four that I cannot understand:

the way of an eagle in the sky, 
the way of a snake on a rock, 
the way of a ship at sea, 
and the way of a man with a {{almah|maiden}}.

This is the way of an adulteress: She eats and wipes her mouth 
and says, 'I have done nothing wrong.'

units.label: Small creatures, exceedingly wise
units.note: the earth trembles under four things

verses.text: Under three things the earth trembles, under four it cannot bear up:

a servant who becomes king, 
a fool who is filled with food,

an unloved woman who marries, 
and a maidservant who supplants her mistress.
Four things on earth are small, yet they are exceedingly {{chakam|wise}}:
The ants are creatures of little strength, yet they store up their food in the summer;
the rock badgers are creatures of little power, yet they make their homes in the rocks;
the locusts have no king, yet they all advance in formation;
and the lizard can be caught in one's hands, yet it is found in the palaces of kings.

units.label: Stately creatures and self-exaltation
units.note: the stirring of anger brings forth strife

verses.text: There are three things that are stately in their stride, and four that are impressive in their walk:
a lion, mighty among beasts, refusing to retreat before anything;

If you have foolishly exalted yourself or if you have plotted evil, 
put your hand over your mouth.

For as the churning of milk yields butter, and the twisting of the nose draws blood, 
so the stirring of anger brings forth strife."

eloah.gloss: God, a singular form related to Elohim, often used in poetic and wisdom literature, notably throughout Job. Verse 5 says every word of this God is flawless, a shield to those who take refuge in Him, grounding Agur's confessed ignorance, verse 3, in trust that God's own revealed word can be relied on completely even when human understanding cannot.

almah.gloss: A young woman of marriageable age, maiden. Verse 19 lists the way of a man with an almah among wonders too great to understand, the same Hebrew word famously used in Isaiah 7:14 of the virgin who would bear Immanuel, showing how ordinary human wonder and covenant promise can share a single word.

chakam.gloss: Wise, skilled in living rightly. Verse 24 calls the ant, the rock badger, the locust, and the lizard 'exceedingly wise' despite their smallness or weakness, teaching that true wisdom is measured by fittingness to one's calling and diligence, not by size, strength, or status.

basic.context: A new and distinct voice speaks in this chapter, Agur son of Jakeh, who is otherwise unknown in Scripture. He opens with a startling confession of his own ignorance before the incomprehensible God, prays simply for honest daily bread rather than poverty or riches, and then teaches through a series of vivid numerical riddles, three or four things, that train the eye to see both the horror of certain evils and the humble wisdom written into small creatures.
basic.hermeneutics: Agur's confessed ignorance, verse 2 to 3, is not false modesty but the honest starting point of real wisdom, since he immediately turns to trust God's flawless word, verse 5, rather than his own understanding. The numerical sayings, three things, four things, are a poetic device common in ancient wisdom literature, building suspense and listing examples that share a common feature, not a rigid mathematical formula.
basic.originalLanguages: Agur names God eloah, verse 5, the same poetic name used often in Job, and confesses total confidence in His flawless word even while confessing his own ignorance of the Holy One, verse 3. The almah, young woman, of verse 19, is the identical Hebrew word Isaiah later uses of the virgin who will bear Immanuel, 7:14, though here it simply names the wonder of a man's courtship, a linguistic link worth noting without overclaiming a direct prophecy in this context.
basic.typology: Agur's rhetorical question, 'what is His name, and what is the name of His Son,' verse 4, anticipates the fuller revelation of God the Father and God the Son that Scripture only later makes explicit, though Agur himself could not have grasped the incarnation. His prayer for neither poverty nor riches, verse 8, foreshadows Jesus' own teaching to pray for daily bread, not accumulated wealth, Matthew 6:11.
basic.christ: Agur's haunting question, 'what is His name, and what is the name of His Son, surely you know,' verse 4, stands as one of the Old Testament's most striking anticipations of the Father-Son relationship within God, fully unveiled only in the incarnation of Jesus Christ, the Son who alone has made the Father known, John 1:18. And Agur's simple prayer for daily bread rather than poverty or riches, verse 8, echoes forward into the Lord's Prayer, where Jesus teaches His disciples to ask their Father for exactly this, 'give us this day our daily bread,' Matthew 6:11.
basic.god: God is the Holy One whom no human wisdom can fully grasp, verse 3, yet every word He speaks is utterly flawless and a shield to those who take refuge in Him, verse 5. He is also the giver of daily bread who hears the simple prayer of a man who wants neither the temptation of riches nor the desperation of poverty, verse 8, showing His care extends to the ordinary, daily needs of His people.
basic.crossReferences: John 1:18 answers Agur's question about the name of God's Son. Matthew 6:11 echoes the prayer for daily bread in verse 8. Job 38:4-11 parallels the rhetorical questions of verse 4 about who has measured creation. Psalm 18:30 echoes the flawless word of God as a shield, verse 5.
basic.oneStory: Agur confesses that true wisdom begins in humility before the incomprehensible God, trusts God's flawless word completely, and asks simply for daily bread rather than poverty or riches. His unanswered question about the name of God's Son finds its answer centuries later in Jesus Christ, the Son who alone reveals the Father and teaches His people to pray for exactly the bread Agur asked for.

context.literary:
Proverbs 30 is a small book inside a book. The collection that ran from 25:1 ended at 29:27, and chapter 30 begins with a new title and a new voice. Its architecture is deliberate. A confession of ignorance and a creed about the word of God open it, verses 1 to 6. A two part prayer follows, verses 7 to 9. Then comes a long run of observations, verses 10 to 33, most of which are built on a pattern of numbers.

The numerical sayings use a device common in the Bible and the wider ancient world, in which a number is named and then raised by one: three things, even four. Amos uses it against the nations, Amos 1:3, and Proverbs 6:16 uses it for the things the LORD hates. In chapter 30 the device appears at 15 and 16, 18 to 19, 21 to 23, 24 to 28 and 29 to 31, and it is always the last item that carries the point. The device is a way of training the eye: the reader is invited to guess the pattern and finds that the fourth thing either completes it or startles.

Another device is repetition. The word generation opens four verses in a row, verses 11 to 14, each introducing a type of person: the one who curses parents, the self righteous, the arrogant and the devouring rich. The word way occurs four times in verse 19 and again in verse 20, joining the wonders of nature to the adulteress.

The chapter ends with a pun that is lost in English. The same Hebrew word means both nose and anger, so churning milk yields butter, twisting the nose yields blood, and stirring anger yields strife, verse 33. The frame is thus complete: a man who begins in humility, verse 2, ends with the advice to cover his mouth, verse 32.
context.historical:
Agur son of Jakeh is not named elsewhere in Scripture, and nothing is known of him beyond this chapter. The title may call his words a burden or oracle, or it may name a place, Massa, which Genesis 25:14 and 1 Chronicles 1:30 list among the sons of Ishmael. If so, Agur was an Arabian wise man, and that fits the wider picture of the Old Testament, where wisdom is sought in Edom and Teman, Jeremiah 49:7, and the book of Job is set in the East. The Bible does not seem troubled by the idea that the Spirit of God could use a voice from the edges of Israel's world.

The prayer of verses 7 to 9 comes from a society where both extremes were real. A good harvest could make a family complacent and a bad one could leave it desperate. Deuteronomy 8:12 to 14 warned that when herds and flocks grew large and silver and gold increased, the heart would become proud and forget the LORD. At the other end, a hungry man might steal, and Agur names that risk.

Verse 17 draws on the culture of honour in the family. The Torah made cursing a parent a capital matter, Exodus 21:17, and a persistent rebel son was brought before the elders, Deuteronomy 21:18 to 21. Having a body left for ravens and vultures was a dreaded curse, Deuteronomy 28:26, because it meant no burial.

The small animals of verses 24 to 28 belong to the Judean landscape: the ant at its harvest store, the rock badger or hyrax in the cliffs, as in Psalm 104:18, the locust swarm that every farmer knew and feared, and a small house lizard or spider found in royal rooms. The list of unbearable things in verses 21 to 23 reads as the fears of a hierarchical society in which a sudden reversal of rank meant chaos.
context.canonical:
The chapter is one of the most densely echoed in the book. Verse 4 gathers the questions that God asks of Job, Job 38, and of Israel in Isaiah 40:12, and every part of it finds an answer in Christ. Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Jesus says that no one has ascended into heaven except the One who descended, John 3:13, and Paul reads the ascent and descent in the same terms, Ephesians 4:9 and 10. Deuteronomy 30:12 had already said that the word is not in heaven, so that no one need ask who will ascend to get it, and Paul applies that to Christ in Romans 10:6 and 7.

Verse 5 is nearly a quotation of Psalm 18:30 and 2 Samuel 22:31, so the ancient creed travelled across the biblical genres. Jesus prays to the Father, 'Your word is truth,' John 17:17. Verse 6, do not add to His words, joins Deuteronomy 4:2 and is reflected in the last warning of the Bible, Revelation 22:18 and 19.

The prayer of verses 8 and 9 has its response in the Lord's Prayer, 'Give us this day our daily bread,' Matthew 6:11, and in the manna of Exodus 16, collected one day at a time. Paul's teaching on contentment, Philippians 4:11 and 12, and 1 Timothy 6:8 and 9 apply the same wisdom to the Church.

Verse 15's insatiable grave is echoed in Habakkuk 2:5. Verses 24 to 28 recall the ant of Proverbs 6:6, and the locusts without a king prompt a comparison with the dark refrain of Judges, where there was no king in Israel, Judges 21:25.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Agur wants his hearers to start from where he starts, with an honest admission of how little they grasp. He is not making a show of modesty. He is saying that a person who has not learned to stand speechless before God has not begun to be wise, and that the world is bigger than the human mind that surveys it. The questions of verse 4 are meant to bring the reader up short: the wind, the waters, the ends of the earth are not ours.

Having put the hearer in his place, Agur gives him something to hold. Every word of God is flawless, verse 5, and the response to it is both trust and restraint, taking refuge in it and not adding to it. The prayer which follows is the practical test of that creed: asking God to keep falsehood away and to give just enough, because a person can lose God through fullness as easily as through want.

The sayings about generations and numbers are meant to train a lived wisdom. Agur wants the hearers to be able to name arrogance, contempt for parents, greed that devours the poor, and the adulterous woman who tidily wipes her mouth. He wants them also to look at small creatures with respect, since wisdom is not the same thing as size or rank.

The warning at the end, if you have exalted yourself or plotted evil, put your hand over your mouth, is a call for the same humility that opened the chapter. It brings the reader back to the posture of verse 2: silence before the truth. Agur's final point is a practical one. Stirring anger, like churning milk, produces something, and the something is strife.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what one man, Agur, said, and it does so without a comment from the editors. That is important for how we read his opening confession. We should not take verse 2, that he is the most ignorant of men, as a doctrine that human beings can know nothing. It is the speech of a person who is overwhelmed by the greatness of God. The prescription behind it is that we also should know ourselves as creatures before the Creator.

Most of the sayings describe. The generations of verses 11 to 14 are warnings and not instructions, and the wonders of verses 18 and 19 simply invite the reader to wonder. The unbearable things in verses 21 to 23 should not be read as a rule that servants may never rise or that unloved women should not marry. They state what a nervous society feared, and their sting is the character of the person who rises: a servant who becomes king without wisdom, a fool filled with food, a woman bitter in a household, a maid who displaces her mistress. Scripture elsewhere rejoices when the lowly are lifted up, 1 Samuel 2:8, and Joseph the servant became a ruler. The warnings are about character, not rank.

What does carry forward are the prayer for neither poverty nor riches, the call to trust God's word without addition, the lesson from the ant and the badger, and the discipline of silence before a rising temper. The prayer is a model and not a law: Scripture does not forbid believers to be rich or poor, but it teaches us to watch what either condition does to the heart.

debates.question: Is Agur's question in verse 4, 'what is His name, and what is the name of His Son,' a direct prophecy of the Trinity and the incarnate Son of God?

views.label: A direct, intentional messianic prophecy of the divine Son
views.case: Some read the parallel between God's name and 'His Son's' name as Agur, under inspiration, glimpsing the plurality within God's own being that the New Testament later reveals fully in the Father and the Son.

views.label: A rhetorical device asserting God's incomprehensibility, later filled with fuller meaning
views.case: In context, Agur's string of questions, who has ascended to heaven, gathered the wind, bound the waters, functions rhetorically to establish that no human, and by extension no human's son, has done these things, only God; the phrase most likely functioned in its original setting as an assertion that God's identity and being are beyond any human's or human family's grasp, a meaning Scripture's later revelation of the Father and the Son fills with unforeseen depth without requiring Agur to have understood the Trinity explicitly.

debates.bearing: Whichever reading is preferred, the New Testament's later revelation of the Father and the Son, John 1:18, gives Agur's ancient, deliberately unanswerable question its truest and fullest answer, an answer Agur himself could not have supplied but that the whole of Scripture was moving toward.

debates.question: Who is speaking in verses 1 to 4, and is the tone humble confession or sceptical challenge?

views.label: Agur confesses his own ignorance
views.case: The traditional reading takes the words at face value. A weary man admits he has not learned wisdom and does not know the Holy One, asks the unanswerable questions of verse 4, and then turns to God's flawless word in verse 5. This reading fits the Bible's wider teaching that wisdom begins in humility, and it makes sense of the prayer which follows.

views.label: Agur quotes a sceptic and answers him
views.case: Some interpreters hear the opening as the voice of an opponent, a man who claims that no one can know God, and take verse 5 and following as Agur's reply. They note the phrase 'surely you know' and the abrupt shift to 'every word of God.'

views.label: Agur's humility is real but sharpened with irony
views.case: A third view holds that Agur is deliberately overstating his ignorance, in the way of a teacher who undercuts the pretensions of those who think they have mastered wisdom. His claim not to know is the lead in to the challenge of verse 4, which no one can answer by their own cleverness.

debates.bearing: The BSB footnote shows how uncertain the opening Hebrew is, since a slightly different vowel reading gives 'I am weary, O God, but I can prevail.' Under every reading, though, the chapter lands in the same place: the human mind does not master God, and the word of God can be trusted. We can hold the reading loosely and the lesson firmly.

debates.question: Is Agur from Massa, and does it matter?

views.label: Agur is an Israelite writing an oracle
views.case: The Hebrew word massa can mean burden or oracle, the term used for many prophetic messages. On this reading the verse says that these are the words of Agur, the oracle he declared, and no foreign origin need be assumed.

views.label: Agur is from Massa, a land associated with Ishmael's descendants
views.case: Genesis 25:14 and 1 Chronicles 1:30 name Massa among the sons of Ishmael, and the same word follows Lemuel's name in 31:1, which some also read as king of Massa. If so, two non Israelite sages stand at the end of Proverbs, and Israel's wisdom books were open to God's truth found beyond Israel's borders.

debates.bearing: The choice does not change the chapter's theology. If Agur is Arabian, it adds a note of humility to Israel's own wisdom tradition, which already recognises wise men in Edom and the East. If he is an Israelite, the chapter still speaks as a prophetic burden. We cannot be sure, and nothing in the teaching hangs on the answer.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 introduces the speaker with a phrase that in Hebrew literally calls him the oracle of the man, the same shape of phrase Balaam uses of himself in Numbers 24:3. It signals that what follows is not a casual opinion but a solemn declaration. The word that the BSB renders burden is the same word used in the prophets for a weighty message, and, as the footnote says, it may also be a place name.

The confession of verse 2 uses a rare and strong word for ignorant. Agur says he is ba'ar, brutish or senseless, the word the psalmist uses of himself in Psalm 73:22 when he looks back on his bitterness and says he was senseless and ignorant, a brute beast before God. It is a word for a creature that lacks understanding, and it appears in Proverbs 12:1, where the one who hates correction is called ba'ar. Agur is placing himself at the lowest rung of understanding in order to stand under God's word.

Verse 5 says God's word is flawless, from the verb tsaraf, to refine in a furnace. The words of the LORD are likened to silver refined in a furnace in Psalm 12:6. The same root names the crucible in Proverbs 27:21, so that the two chapters are joined: a person is tested by praise as silver by fire, but the word of God has already been refined. The second clause, a shield to those who take refuge, matches Psalm 18:30 almost word for word, which suggests that Agur is reciting a familiar creed of Israel.

Verse 8 asks for bread that is a portion, with a word that comes from chok, something allotted and decreed. It is the language of rations, as in a household where each is given what has been measured out. Agur does not ask for plenty or for scarcity but for the measured daily amount, which is the situation of Israel in the wilderness with the manna, Exodus 16:19 and 20.

Verse 9 puts a question on the lips of the fat man, 'Who is the LORD?' It is Pharaoh's question in Exodus 5:2. A full stomach can lead to the same dismissal of God as a hard heart.

In verse 19, almah is a word for a young woman of marriageable age, used of Rebekah in Genesis 24:43. Genesis 24:16 describes the same girl with another word as a virgin. The same word appears in Isaiah 7:14. The BSB renders it maiden here and virgin in Isaiah, and the context decides the nuance. In Proverbs it simply names the wonder of courtship, and the connection to Isaiah should be left to the New Testament's own use of Isaiah.

Verse 24 describes the small creatures as wise with a doubled form of the root chakam, wise and made wise, as if their wisdom were both given and learned. The ant of Proverbs 6:6 is told to teach the sluggard by the same word wise.

Verse 33 plays on a double sense. The word for nose and the word for anger are the same Hebrew word in different forms, so the line says that pressing the nose brings blood and pressing anger brings strife.

typology.type: The questions about heaven and earth, Proverbs 30:4
typology.fulfillment: Agur asks who has ascended to heaven and come down, who has gathered the wind and bound the waters. Job 38 and Isaiah 40:12 answer that only God does these things. In Christ the questions find a person. He is the One who descended from heaven, John 3:13, and ascended above all the heavens, Ephesians 4:9 and 10. He stilled the wind and sea with a word, Mark 4:39 to 41, and all things hold together in Him, Colossians 1:16 and 17. The type is a question with no human answer, and Christ is the answer, though the original author may not have foreseen it.

typology.type: Every word of God is flawless, Proverbs 30:5
typology.fulfillment: The refined word of the LORD that is a shield for those who take refuge is embodied in the Son, who is the Word, John 1:1 and 14. He upholds all things by His powerful word, Hebrews 1:3, and He prays, 'Your word is truth,' John 17:17. In the wilderness He shielded Himself with it against the tempter, 'It is written,' Matthew 4:4. The correspondence is real, since the written word and the living Word agree. It falls short only in that the written word points ahead and the Word made flesh fulfils.

typology.type: Neither poverty nor riches, only bread, Proverbs 30:8
typology.fulfillment: Agur's prayer for a measured portion looks forward to the prayer Jesus teaches, 'Give us this day our daily bread,' Matthew 6:11, and back to the manna that came a day at a time, Exodus 16. In Jesus the pattern is a life lived entirely on the Father's daily provision. He had nowhere to lay His head, Luke 9:58, yet He fed the crowds, Mark 6:41 to 44, and called Himself the bread of life, John 6:35. Agur's prayer is a request for daily bread, and Jesus is the one who is bread, so the escalation is from provision to the Provider.

typology.type: The small and wise, Proverbs 30:24 to 28
typology.fulfillment: The ants, badgers, locusts and lizard are small, yet wise. Scripture often shows God choosing the weak to shame the strong, as Paul observes in 1 Corinthians 1:27. Jesus was born in a stable, came from a town of little reputation, John 1:46, and told His followers to become like children, Matthew 18:3. The correspondence is not a hidden prediction. It lies in the way the Lord reverses the world's measure of greatness. The type falls short because the animals are wise by instinct, and Christ's followers are made wise by grace.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ in the most direct way through verse 4, with a fair and a cautious reading of it.

The fair part comes first. Agur asks four questions about the Creator and a fifth about His name and His Son's name. The first four are answered everywhere in the Old Testament by God alone: He gathers the wind, Psalm 135:7, He measures the waters in the hollow of His hand, Isaiah 40:12. The New Testament says that the One who did these things is the Son. He is before all things, and all things were created through Him and hold together in Him, Colossians 1:16 and 17. He upholds all things by His powerful word, Hebrews 1:3. The disciples ask, 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?' Mark 4:41. They are asking the question of Proverbs 30:4 in the first person. And as for the question about ascent and descent, it is the Son who came down and went up, John 3:13 and Ephesians 4:9 and 10.

The cautious part belongs to the end of the verse. When Agur asks what God's name is and what His son's name is, he does not say what he means, and the sentence reads naturally as a challenge to the human mind: you cannot name Him, and you cannot name the one who inherits. That the reader of the whole Bible hears more in it does not require that Agur did. Psalm 2:7 introduces the Son of God in a royal setting, and John 1:18 and Matthew 11:27 say that only the Son has made the Father known. Together they supply the answer that the proverb leaves open, though the proverb alone does not.

Verse 5 leads to Christ through the written word. The one who is a shield to those who take refuge is also the one in whom the refuge is found, and the psalm Agur echoes opens by calling the LORD a rock and a fortress, Psalm 18:2. And the prayer of verse 8 leads to Christ in the form He gave it, with daily bread in the Lord's Prayer, Matthew 6:11, and later in the declaration that He Himself is the bread of life, John 6:35.

Agur's humility is also a gospel theme: it is the poor in spirit who receive the kingdom, Matthew 5:3, and those who admit they do not know are the ones to whom the Son chooses to reveal the Father, Matthew 11:25 to 27.

One caution applies. The sayings about eagles, snakes and ants are not allegories of the Saviour. They train the eye. It is the questions and the creed that point beyond themselves.
study.god:
Agur's God is first of all beyond comprehension. The Holy One, verse 3, is one whose ways and being lie outside human grasp. The questions of verse 4 are the language of transcendence: heaven is His home, the wind and waters are His instruments, the ends of the earth are His foundation. Nothing in the chapter reduces Him to a doctrine we can master.

Yet this same God is not silent. The most striking move in the chapter is the move from verse 4 to verse 5, from an unanswerable question to a flawless word. The God who cannot be seen from the earth has spoken, and His speech is refined, as silver is refined in a furnace. This is the central tension of the chapter, that God is both utterly beyond us and utterly reliable. It holds together His hiddenness and His self disclosure, and it forbids both agnosticism and presumption. We cannot add to His words, verse 6, because they are complete in what they say, and we may not ignore them because they are His.

He is a shield for those who take refuge in Him. The image is military and intimate: He stands between the believer and harm, and the believer runs to Him. The line is borrowed from Israel's psalmody, Psalm 18:30, which says something about how God's people prayed. They carried the creed in their mouths.

He is the giver of the daily portion, who hears a prayer about ordinary needs. Agur's request for neither poverty nor riches is a confession about the human heart, that it can be damaged by plenty and by want, and about God's good ordering of our lives. His provision is measured and fitting, just as the manna was.

He is also the Judge who exposes the self righteous, the arrogant and the oppressors of verses 12 to 14 and who sees the adulteress who wipes her mouth, verse 20. The God who sets limits on pride is the same one who gives wisdom to ants.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to begin where Agur does, in weariness and ignorance, and to move to the sure word. It also teaches us to pray small prayers, for honesty and bread, without embarrassment.

crossReferences.note: God asks Job where he was when the earth's foundations were laid and who shut in the sea. These are the questions of verse 4 posed by the Creator Himself, and they show that Agur's ignorance is the right response to the questions only God can answer.

Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, marked off the heavens and weighed the mountains? Isaiah uses the pictures of verse 4 to humble the nations and comfort Israel, and shows the same confidence that the Creator is beyond measure.
The word of the LORD is flawless, and He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him. Verse 5 is almost a quotation, which suggests Agur is reciting a creed that Israel already prayed in its psalms.
Do not add to or subtract from what the LORD commands. Verse 6 echoes this guard on the word, and the Bible's last chapter, Revelation 22:18 and 19, repeats the same warning for the whole book.

When you eat and are satisfied, and your herds and silver increase, your heart will become proud and you will forget the LORD. It is the danger Agur names in verse 9, that the full will say, 'Who is the LORD?'

Pharaoh's answer to Moses: 'Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice?' The same question appears on the lips of the satisfied man in verse 9, which ties the temptation of wealth to the spirit of Egypt.

'Give us this day our daily bread.' Jesus' model prayer takes up the request of verse 8 and places it among the petitions of the kingdom, which suggests that Agur asked for what God intends all His children to ask.

Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, nor are the eyes of man. The same insatiable grave appears in 30:16, and the earlier chapter's observation about the eye clarifies the greed behind the leech's daughters, Give and Give.

The sluggard is told to consider the ant, which has no commander yet prepares its food in summer. Agur's ants in verse 25 repeat the lesson with less to say about the lazy and more about the humble wisdom of small things.
No one has ascended into heaven except the One who descended from heaven, the Son of Man. It supplies the answer to the first question of verse 4, who has ascended and come down.

All things were created through the Son and for Him, and in Him all things hold together. It reads the cosmic questions of verse 4 as pointing to the Son, a reading the proverb itself does not make but the New Testament does.

In those days there was no king in Israel. The locusts that march in formation without a king, verse 27, make a pointed contrast to a people who without a king each did what was right in his own eyes.

study.oneStory:
Proverbs 30 comes from the edge of Israel's world, and it speaks to the questions that stand at the beginning of the Bible. Genesis asks who made the earth and the wind and waters, and Agur's questions in verse 4 take us back to that creation story. The answer in Genesis is that God spoke and it was so. The question of whether a human being can know such a God is one that Eden raised, when the serpent suggested that knowledge could be seized, and Agur's reply is to refuse the grasp and receive the word.

The prayer for neither poverty nor riches is also an Eden prayer. In the garden everything was given as a daily gift, and the fall began with a reach for more. Agur's fear that fullness will say 'Who is the LORD?' is the same thing in later dress, and so is Israel's story in the wilderness, where manna was given a day at a time and hoarding rotted. The manna is the pattern for a life lived on what God provides.

The sayings about generations, insatiable appetites and the pride of the strutting king are portraits of the fallen world. Sheol is never full, and the sin of mocking parents and devouring the poor has not stopped. Yet the creatures of verses 24 to 28 witness to a world that still carries the order of the Creator: the ants gather, the badgers shelter, the locusts keep ranks.

The story moves on in the same direction as the chapter, from questions to a Person. The Son who descended and ascended, who stilled the wind and sea, and who taught His people to pray for daily bread, answers Agur's longing. In Him every word of God is shown to be true.

The new creation will end the questions. We will see His face, Revelation 22:4, and the throne of God and of the Lamb will be among us, Revelation 22:3. The weariness of verse 1 will be over, and the unquenchable hunger of the grave will have been answered by a feast, for death will be no more, Revelation 21:4.

quiz.q: What does Agur confess about himself in verses 2 to 3?

options.text: That he is the most ignorant of men and has no knowledge of the Holy One.
options.note: Agur begins his oracle with humble self-assessment rather than a claim to superior wisdom.

options.text: That he possesses more wisdom than any other man.
options.note: This is the opposite of his actual confession.

options.text: That he understands the natural world perfectly.
options.note: His confession is about spiritual and theological ignorance, not merely natural science.

options.text: That he is moderately wise but still has room to grow.
options.note: His language is much stronger, calling himself the most ignorant, not merely moderately wise.

quiz.q: What does verse 5 say about every word of God?

options.text: It is flawless, and He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him.
options.note: Confidence in God's word grounds Agur's confessed personal ignorance.

options.text: It requires human correction and refinement.
options.note: This is the opposite of calling God's word flawless.

options.text: It applies only to ancient Israel, not to all people.
options.note: The verse makes a universal claim about God's word, not a limited one.

options.text: It is mostly reliable but occasionally uncertain.
options.note: The verse's claim is absolute, 'flawless,' not partial reliability.

quiz.q: What two things does Agur ask for in verses 7 to 9?

options.text: That falsehood be kept far from him, and that he be given neither poverty nor riches, but his daily bread.
options.note: Agur prays for honesty and contented, sufficient provision.

options.text: Great wealth and a long life.
options.note: This is essentially the opposite of what Agur actually requests.

options.text: Forgiveness of sins and eternal life.
options.note: While these are legitimate biblical requests elsewhere, they are not what this specific prayer asks for.

options.text: Poverty alone, to prove his humility.
options.note: Agur specifically asks to avoid both poverty and riches, not to embrace poverty deliberately.

quiz.q: According to verses 24-28, what quality do the ant, rock badger, locust, and lizard share despite being small or weak?

options.text: They are exceedingly wise.
options.note: Wisdom in these small creatures is shown through fittingness to their calling, not strength or size.

options.text: They are the strongest creatures on earth.
options.note: The text specifically calls them creatures of little strength or power.

options.text: They are dangerous predators.
options.note: This is not the point being made about these creatures.

options.text: They are wise only because of their size advantage.
options.note: The passage's point is the opposite, that their wisdom is impressive precisely despite their small size or weakness.

quiz.q: What does verse 32 instruct if you have foolishly exalted yourself or plotted evil?

options.text: Put your hand over your mouth.
options.note: Self-restraint and silence are urged as the appropriate response to recognized folly or evil scheming.

options.text: Announce your plans publicly to gain support.
options.note: This is the opposite of the restraint the verse calls for.

options.text: Seek immediate revenge on your rivals.
options.note: The verse's counsel is self-restraint, not aggression toward others.

options.text: Wait a few days before taking further action.
options.note: The verse's specific instruction is silence, putting a hand over the mouth, not merely a delay before continuing.

questions: Agur begins by confessing his own ignorance before God, verses 2-3. Where do you need to admit the limits of your own understanding rather than pretending to have it all figured out?
Agur prays for neither poverty nor riches, only his daily bread, verse 8. Where is your own desire for either comfort or wealth putting your dependence on God at risk?
Agur's question about the name of God's Son, verse 4, is answered centuries later in Jesus. How does knowing the Son's name change the way you read Agur's honest confession of ignorance?
The small creatures of verses 24-28 are called wise despite being weak or small. Where might you be underestimating your own capacity to be faithful simply because you feel small or insignificant?

Verse 32 counsels silence, a hand over the mouth, after foolish self-exaltation or plotting. Is there a recent moment of pride or scheming in your own heart that calls for this kind of humble silence before God?

translationNotes.note: 'Agur son of Jakeh' and the recipients 'Ithiel' and 'Ucal' are obscure; some ancient versions and modern scholars read the Hebrew consonants differently, yielding 'I am weary, O God, I am weary and worn out,' as reflected in this BSB rendering, rather than treating Ithiel and Ucal as proper names throughout.

The rhetorical question 'What is His name, and what is the name of His Son' uses the Hebrew word ben, son, without further explanation in its immediate context, leaving its fullest meaning for later revelation to unfold.
'The leech has two daughters: Give and Give' is a proverbial image for insatiable demand, introducing the numerical list of things that are never satisfied that follows in verse 16.
